NeoDoc

plain text for the atmosphere

Overview

NeoDoc is a plain-text format for creating, storing, and querying content. It's easy to write without sacrificing the power to make full-featured posts and pages. Basically, it's markdown on steroids with a free-form database thrown in for good measure.

NeoDoc provides a clean separation of concerns between layouts and content. Individual apps are in complete control over what they render. Everything becomes extremely portable as a result. Even better, the content is organized into sections with optional attributes. The combination provides the foundation of a queryable interface.

Apps can make custom displays of individual posts or aggregate content from across the atmosphere to provide unique views of the world.

How It Works

Content and Templates

For a quick example, here's a NeoDoc for a monthly book review post:

-- title

Books From July

Family reunion time. Always a good opportunity 
to get some reading done down by the water. 
Here's what I got up to:

-- book-review
-- author: Matt Dinniman
-- cover: dungeon-crawler-carl-cover.jpg

Dungeon Crawler Carl

First off, I did the audio book instead of the 
paper copy. I don't know how much I would have 
liked the physical version but the narrator for 
the audio book is absolute gold. etc.

-- book-review
-- author: William Gibson 
-- cover: neuromancer-cover.jpg

Neuromancer

The Matrix, you say? Have I got a story for you. 
etc.
It turns into this:

Books From July

Family reunion time. Always a good opportunity to get some reading done down by the water. Here's what I got up to:

Dungeon Crawler Carl
by Matt Dinniman

First off, I did the audio book instead of the paper copy. I don't know how much I would have liked the physical version but the narrator for the audio book is absolute gold. etc.

Neuromancer
by William Gibson

The Matrix, you say? Have I got a story for you. etc.

The formatting comes from HTML templates applied by the app that's rendering the content. Since each app can have its own templates, another one could pick up the same content and render it like this:

Books From July

Family reunion time. Always a good opportunity to get some reading done down by the water. Here's what I got up to:

Dungeon Crawler Carl
[Matt Dinniman]

First off, I did the audio book instead of the paper copy. I don't know how much I would have liked the physical version but the narrator for the audio book is absolute gold. etc.

Neuromancer
[William Gibson]

The Matrix, you say? Have I got a story for you. etc.

Graceful Defaults

NeoDocs are collections of content broken up into sections. Each one starts with two dashes and a name. For example, there's a single "-- title" and two "-- book-review" sections in the example above. (The book-review sections also have a couple lines of attributes after the header. We'll get to those momentarily.)

NeoDoc generates HTML by matching section names to templates. That's how each of the hypothetical apps above created their view of the content. However, there's no guarantee that any given app will have a template for a specific section type. NeoDoc handles those cases by falling back to rendering sections without templates as paragraphs.

So, an app without -- title or -- book-review templates would render the monthly review post like this:

Books From July

Family reunion time. Always a good opportunity to get some reading done down by the water. Here's what I got up to:

Dungeon Crawler Carl

First off, I did the audio book instead of the paper copy. I don't know how much I would have liked the physical version but the narrator for the audio book is absolute gold. etc.

Neuromancer

The Matrix, you say? Have I got a story for you. etc.

The Attributes

Each of the -- book-review sections in the example has additions lines starting with two dashes. Specifically, the -- author and -- cover lines. These are section attributes. Each one consists of a key/value pair.

Attribute content doesn't appear by default That's why the authors and cover images don't show up in the fallback, paragraph view of the content. It's up to individual apps to include the content or not as they see fit.

But, attributes offer more than just the ability to appear in the output. They provide data that can be queried.

The NeoDoc Database

NeoDoc's sections and attributes create the foundation of queryable, ad hoc database. For example, say you have a piece of content with a hundred -- book-review sections in it. Each one with an -- author attribute. You could write an app that lets you search for and display all the apps from a given author.

There's no reason the query has to be limited to a single file. The app could be set up to query against all your posts looking for any -- book-review with an -- author of the given name.

Going the next step up, there's no reason the app has to be limited to just your content. With the public, open nature of the Atmosphere, you can query everything that's in any NeoDoc out there.

Current Status

The NeoDoc format has been around for three years. You've probably never heard of it, though. That's because it's embedded in my personal static site generator. I'm in the process of extracting the parser into a library and creating a reference implementation. I don't have an ETA, but it won't be too long.

You can follow me or the neodoc.style accounts for updates.

In the mean time, I'll see you in the Atmosphere.
